newsitem.title: USA: IBM says researchers devise tough encryption code.
newsitem.headline: IBM says researchers devise tough encryption code.

text.p: International Busines Machines Corp. said on Wednesday two of its researchers have created an encryption system that keeps confidential computer data private with a uniform level of protection.
However, IBM said the encryption system was more scientific than practical at this point.

Encryption products, which scramble information and render it unreadable without a password or software "key," have become an increasingly important component of global communications and online commerce over the Internet.

"This is a pioneering accomplishment in the field of cryptography and a big step toward the ultimate in cryptography -- a truly invincible mathematically proven method for protecting private computer information from unwanted viewing," said Ashok Chandra, manager of computer science at IBM's Almaden Research Centre in San Jose, Calif.
The system was invented by computer scientists Miklos Ajtai and Cynthia Dwork of IBM's Almaden lab.
The IBM encryption system generates hundreds of random codes, each of which is difficult to decode, to protect information from electronic eavesdroppers, the company said.

The system is based on a mathematical problem that has long eluded mathematicians, IBM said. Once a practical system is developed, its complexity could be expanded, which would make solving the underlying problem even more difficult, it added.
